subject: History
source: National Curriculum KS2 (a non-European society that provides contrasts with British history: early Islamic civilisation, including Baghdad c. AD 900); no school Drive history material found for Y6, written from scratch

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Early Islamic civilisation and Baghdad c. AD 900
lessons.title: The Abbasid Caliphate and the founding of Baghdad
objectives: Explain how the Islamic world grew after the time of the Prophet, peace be upon him
Describe why Baghdad was founded and how it was planned

keywords.def: the leader of the Muslim community and state
the dynasty of caliphs who ruled from Baghdad from AD 750
the capital city founded in AD 762 beside the River Tigris
a developed society with cities, government and culture

starter: Which two groups fought for England in the 800s?
Why is it important to use more than one source?

teach.heading: Bismillah: a great civilisation
bullets: While Britain faced Vikings, Baghdad was thriving
The Islamic world stretched from Spain to Central Asia
We study c. AD 900, over 1,100 years ago
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Compare with Year 5: ask what was happening in Britain around AD 900 (Alfred's successors, Vikings) and show the contrast. Check pupils know the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, lived in the 7th century CE.

teach.heading: The Abbasid Caliphate
bullets: The Abbasids came to power in AD 750
Their capital moved east from Damascus
Caliphs ruled a huge empire of many peoples
teach.note: Be accurate and respectful: the Abbasids followed the Umayyads. The empire included Arabs, Persians, Berbers, Christians, Jews and others. Mention that many languages and cultures contributed to the civilisation.

teach.heading: Why Baghdad?
bullets: Caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad in AD 762
It stood on the River Tigris
Rivers and trade routes made it a rich location
teach.note: Show a map. Ask why a river location helps a city: water, farming, transport, trade. Al-Mansur chose the site carefully, according to historians.

teach.heading: The Round City
bullets: The first city was circular
Its walls were about 2.5 kilometres across
The caliph's palace stood at the centre
teach.note: The Round City of Baghdad, also called Madinat al-Salam (City of Peace), had gates facing different directions. Don't claim precise measurements beyond 'about'. Ask what might a round design show about the ruler.

practice: Name two reasons Baghdad was a good place for a capital.
independent: Label a map of the Abbasid Caliphate with Baghdad, Damascus, Cordoba and the River Tigris
Draw the Round City and add four labels
Write 5 sentences explaining why the Abbasids built Baghdad
exit: In which year was Baghdad founded?
Give one reason why a river helps a city grow.
lessons.homework: Ask someone at home how Baghdad or another Islamic city has been important in history and share one fact.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: labelled map outline with a word bank. Stretch: compare Baghdad with London in c. AD 900 using two criteria.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Early Islamic civilisation and Baghdad c. AD 900
lessons.title: The House of Wisdom and the love of knowledge
objectives: Explain what the House of Wisdom was
Describe why learning was so important in the Islamic world

keywords.def: the great centre of learning and translation in Baghdad
changing writing from one language into another
a person who has studied a subject deeply
a material for writing, made from plant fibres

starter: Why was Baghdad built on the Tigris?

teach.heading: Seeking knowledge
bullets: The first word revealed to the Prophet was Iqra, read
Muslims were encouraged to seek knowledge
Learning became part of daily life
teach.note: The first revelation, in Surah al-Alaq (96:1), begins with 'Iqra', meaning 'Read' or 'Recite'. Also point out Surah Ta-Ha 20:114: 'My Lord, increase me in knowledge.' Cite plainly and with respect.

teach.heading: The House of Wisdom
bullets: Baghdad had a great library and study centre
It grew greatly under Caliph al-Ma'mun (813-833)
Scholars gathered from many lands
teach.note: Historians debate exactly how the institution worked, so say 'a centre of learning and translation'. Avoid overstating specifics. Ask pupils what a library today offers that is the same.

teach.heading: The translation movement
bullets: Greek, Persian and Indian books were translated into Arabic
Scholars added their own discoveries
Knowledge was shared across languages
teach.note: Explain that translators like Hunayn ibn Ishaq worked on Greek medical books. Stress the Islamic world not only preserved but improved and added new knowledge.

teach.heading: Paper changes everything
bullets: Paper was cheaper than parchment
Paper mills opened in Baghdad around AD 794
More books could be made and sold
teach.note: Knowledge of papermaking came from China. Ask pupils how cheaper paper helps spread knowledge, like printing and the internet later. Booksellers' markets (warraqin) were found in Baghdad.

practice: What was translated in the House of Wisdom?
independent: Draw an inside view of the House of Wisdom with scholars, books and translators
Write a diary entry of a scholar visiting Baghdad
Make a flow chart: Greek book, translated into Arabic, new ideas, shared again
exit: Name one thing scholars did in the House of Wisdom.
How did paper help spread knowledge?
lessons.homework: Ask a family member about a scholar or teacher who inspired them and report back one thing they learned.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pictures with key words for the flow chart. Stretch: explain why sharing knowledge across languages leads to new discoveries.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Early Islamic civilisation and Baghdad c. AD 900
lessons.title: Scholars and scientists of the golden age
objectives: Describe the work of at least two Muslim scholars
Explain how their ideas still affect us today

keywords.def: a branch of mathematics using letters and symbols for unknown numbers
a mathematician of Baghdad whose book gave algebra its name
a physician and scientist of Baghdad, known as Rhazes in Europe
a place where sick people are cared for by doctors

starter: What was the House of Wisdom?

teach.heading: Al-Khwarizmi
bullets: He lived about AD 780 to 850
He worked in the House of Wisdom
His book on solving equations named algebra
teach.note: The word algebra comes from 'al-jabr' in the title of his book. Our word algorithm comes from his name. Show a simple equation, e.g. x + 3 = 10, and ask pupils to solve it: that is algebra.

teach.heading: Numbers we use
bullets: Hindu-Arabic numerals include zero
Scholars explained how to use them
They spread to Europe and replaced Roman numerals
teach.note: The numerals developed in India and were explained and spread by scholars including al-Khwarizmi. Ask pupils to compare 1999 with MCMXCIX in Roman numerals.

teach.heading: Al-Razi and medicine
bullets: Al-Razi lived about AD 854 to 925
He wrote many books on medicine
He worked in hospitals in Baghdad and Rayy
teach.note: Al-Razi wrote about measles and smallpox and insisted on careful observation. Hospitals (bimaristans) cared for the sick, including those who couldn't pay. Link to compassion and caring for the sick in Islam.

teach.heading: Building and learning for all
bullets: Fatima al-Fihri founded al-Qarawiyyin in Fez in AD 859
It is one of the oldest universities
Education was open to many people
teach.note: Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco, was founded by Fatima al-Fihri and is considered one of the world's oldest continually operating universities. Ask: why did she build it? Compare with TGA and school today.

practice: Which word comes from al-Khwarizmi's book title?
Name one thing al-Razi did for medicine.
independent: Make a 'Famous Scholars' fact file for al-Khwarizmi and al-Razi
Write a paragraph: which scholar's work do you think matters most today?
Complete a table of discoveries and how they help us today
lessons.homework: Find one thing in your home or school that uses numbers or maths and explain how algebra or numerals help.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: fact file with images and word bank. Stretch: explain why one scholar's work could not have happened without translated books.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Early Islamic civilisation and Baghdad c. AD 900
lessons.title: Trade, markets and legacy: Baghdad compared with Britain
objectives: Describe how trade made Baghdad rich
Compare Baghdad with Britain around AD 900

keywords.def: a network of trade routes linking China to the Mediterranean
to show how two things are different

teach.heading: Baghdad's markets
bullets: Merchants traded silk, spices, paper and glass
Goods came from China, India and Africa
The Tigris and caravans carried goods
teach.note: Bismillah. Show an illustration of a souq. Ask what a visitor to Baghdad might see, smell and hear. Link to trade with Muslim merchants as honest dealers, which is encouraged in Islam.

teach.heading: A city of millions?
bullets: Baghdad was one of the largest cities of its time
Estimates suggest several hundred thousand people
It had mosques, schools, hospitals and gardens
teach.note: Population estimates vary, so say 'possibly 500,000 or more'. Compare to London at this time, which probably had far fewer people. Ask: what does a large population tell us?

teach.heading: Britain around AD 900
bullets: Britain had small towns and villages
Alfred's successors fought Viking settlers
Buildings were mostly timber
teach.note: Revisit Year 5 learning. Be fair: Britain had its own skills, such as metalwork, laws and monasteries. The contrast is about scale of cities and ways of learning, not value of people.

teach.heading: Legacy today
bullets: Algebra, numerals and optics came from this age
Universities, hospitals and libraries grew from it
Many English words come from Arabic
teach.note: English words from Arabic include algebra, algorithm, alcohol, sugar, cotton, magazine and coffee. Ask pupils to find any they use. Close with gratitude and dua for beneficial knowledge.

practice: Name two goods traded in Baghdad.
Give one difference between Baghdad and Britain c. AD 900.
Name one English word that comes from Arabic.
independent: Complete a comparison table: Baghdad and Britain for size, learning, trade
Write a postcard from a merchant arriving in Baghdad
Write a conclusion: What was the most important contribution of Baghdad c. AD 900? Explain why
exit: Name two things that made Baghdad rich.
Name one thing we still use today from this civilisation.
lessons.homework: Make a list of five English words that come from Arabic and find what each means.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: comparison table with pictures and sentence stems. Stretch: argue whether 'golden age' is a fair description of Baghdad.
